clue.text: Spy working precisely

parts.note: to spy something is to spot it — catch sight of it across a room
a machine that is working is on, the way a switch is

explanation.walkthrough: Two ordinary words sit side by side with nothing between them, and the surface makes them one job description. Neither is a noun about espionage: one is a verb, one is a setting.
explanation.definitionFit: Spot-on means exactly right — the image is a shot that lands dead on the marked spot rather than near it.

clue.text: Strong liquor: drunkard's called for pics

indicators.note: What a man calls a thing is the sound he makes, and a drinker thickens his consonants, so the sound to write down is a slurred one.

parts.note: pics are snaps, and thickened in the mouth of somebody who has had a few, that one syllable comes out with a German spelling

explanation.walkthrough: The colon works as an equals sign: everything after it is one word said badly. The joke is that the drink and the photographs are the same request once the speaker has been at the bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: Schnapps is a clear distilled spirit from Germany and the Netherlands, drunk in small glasses because of its strength.

clue.text: Nine or three sheets to the wind?

definitions.meaning: read as arithmetic: add a single unit to eight and this is the count you reach
a sailor's phrase for very drunk — the sheets are ropes, and three of them loose leave the boat lurching

explanation.walkthrough: The same fifteen letters are handed over twice, once as a sum and once as an idiom, with 'or' doing nothing but joining them. British pubs supply the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom counts drinks — one past the eight pints a man was supposed to manage — so it means tipsy, while the sum makes the same words mean nine.

clue.text: Primarily obtuse, asinine fathead?

indicators.note: Primarily means at the start, so it asks for the opening letter of each word after it rather than for anything the words mean.

parts.note: its opening letter; obtuse means slow on the uptake
its opening letter; asinine means like an ass
its opening letter; a fathead is a blockhead

explanation.walkthrough: Read once for letters and once for sense: the three insults describe the very person their initials spell, which is what makes the whole clue do both jobs at once.
explanation.definitionFit: Every word here describes a stupid, clumsy sort of man, so the sentence reads straight as a description as well as an instruction.

clue.text: Puddings — anxious — sent back

indicators.note: Goods sent back travel the way they came, so the letters are read off from the far end instead of the near one.

parts.note: somebody anxious is stressed, and that word is turned end for end

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'pudding' names the sweet course whatever is on the plate, so the plural is fair. The pleasure of the clue is that the complaint and the cure are the same eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage pudding is the sweet course of a meal, whatever it is made of, so the two words name one course.

clue.text: Type up welcoming German country

indicators.note: Something that is up is unsettled — up in the air, all shaken up — and letters in that state do not stay in the order they arrived in.
To welcome a guest is to take them in, so the single letter standing for German joins the pile being rearranged.

parts.note: used for its four letters, not for anything it means
G is the dictionary's label for the German language

explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'up' usually lifts a word backwards up the grid, and that reading spells nothing here. It is the looser sense — left unsettled — that the setter wants.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition is the bare category: this north African state is one country among many, which is why no adjective narrows it.

clue.text: Spelled out imperatives, not entirely in public

indicators.note: To spell a word out is to hand over its letters one at a time, and here they come back arranged in a different order.

parts.note: one word supplies all eleven letters wanted, and no others

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not entirely' looks as though it is trimming a letter off the fodder. It belongs to the definition instead — the four words after the comma are one phrase meaning halfway public.
explanation.definitionFit: A semi-private room or garden is open to some people and closed to everyone else, so it is public only halfway.

clue.text: Hesitator, biting unwisely — fish's last action?

indicators.note: To do a thing unwisely is to do it wrongly, and letters handled wrongly end up in places other than their own.

parts.note: fifteen letters between those two words, exactly the fifteen the grid wants

explanation.walkthrough: 'Biting unwisely' describes the phrase so neatly that it reads as the definition, which is the trap: it is the raw material, and the definition is the angler's view from the bank.
explanation.definitionFit: A fish that rises to the bait takes the hook, so it really is its last act; the phrase also means reacting to a provocation.

clue.text: American pastries rejected, more than one rank

indicators.note: To reject a thing is to send it back where it came from, so the assembled letters are read from the other end.

parts.note: A is the dictionary's short form for American
tarts are pastries, open cases with jam or fruit in them

explanation.walkthrough: 'More than one' is a nudge that the answer is already a plural, of the Latin kind that does not end in S. 'Rank' is the layer sense — a level of society, not a military grade.
explanation.definitionFit: Strata are layers, in rock or in society, and a social stratum is a level people are ranked in — one word, many layers.

clue.text: Cake-burner not finishing half of scones: like a picnic?

parts.note: King Alfred, who in the old English story was left to watch a peasant woman's cakes and let them char, minus his last letter
the first three of its six letters

explanation.walkthrough: Cakes and scones keep one baking scene running from end to end, and only the first of them is about a person at all — the second is in the clue for three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Al fresco means out in the open air, from the Italian, and eating outdoors is exactly what a picnic is.

clue.text: Henry necessarily not beginning in attentive manner

parts.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of electrical inductance
NEEDFULLY means necessarily, with its opening N gone

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the surface hints at physics, which is the trick: a man's first name shrunk to a single letter is one of the cheapest disguises a setter has.
explanation.definitionFit: To heed is to pay attention, so doing something heedfully is doing it with your attention on it — the adverb of that verb.

clue.text: Flipping Everyman's ultimately parsimonious: code for 'skinflint'

indicators.note: flipping means turning over, so the letters of I'm run backwards

parts.note: the setter, Everyman, is saying I am, shortened to I'm

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so each word gives its last letter

parts.note: the three words whose final letters are taken

explanation.surface: The setter declares, with feeling, that being tight-fisted is a byword for meanness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' applies to all three words, parsimonious, code and for, giving S, E and R.
explanation.definitionFit: A miser hoards money and hates spending it, exactly what a skinflint does.

clue.text: I recommend Bill gets protection from sun

definitions.note: The definition is a line of speech rather than a noun. The setter names the person by the words that come out of their mouth, so the answer is whoever says them for a living.

parts.note: a bill pasted on a wall is an advertisement, an ad
the stiff peak on a cap, or the flap you pull down in a car

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' reads as a man being told to wear a hat, and the capital letter sells it. It is the poster sense, which is why the shortest word in the clue carries two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An advisor's whole job is saying what should be done, so a sentence opening 'I recommend' is that person at work.

clue.text: Social event that's hardly a ball!

definitions.meaning: the straight half: this really is a party with music, held in a hall with a caller shouting the moves to sets of four couples
two senses in four words — a formal dance IS a ball, and yet the shape this one is named after is the least round thing there is

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark sells disappointment: hardly a ball, meaning hardly any fun. The setter means it geometrically, and the event he is describing is a ball after all.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue defines it: a barn-dance party where couples form sets of four, so the shape in its name is the joke against 'ball'.

clue.text: King wearing t-shirt, perhaps, not 'man-bun'-style hairdo

indicators.note: wearing means having on, so the top goes around the letter for king

parts.note: a T-shirt is an example of a top
taken as written
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A king in casual clothes does not go for a trendy bun hairstyle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' marks the T-shirt as one example of a top.
explanation.definitionFit: A topknot is hair gathered in a knot on the crown, which is how a man bun is worn.

clue.text: Musician wanted for buffets?

definitions.meaning: the honest half of the clue: whoever this is, they play in the band and are being hired for it
a buffet is also a blow — the wind buffets a ship — so what is being advertised for is somebody to hit things

explanation.walkthrough: Read the last word as the cold table and the clue books a player for a party. The other buffet is a battering, and delivering those all evening is the job.
explanation.definitionFit: This player is the one who strikes things — drums, cymbals, triangle — so a musician hired to deliver blows is exactly the trade named.

clue.text: Noted repeatedly concerning electrical component

indicators.note: It says the word after it is to be used twice over, once for each of the two short synonyms that word has.

parts.note: a book on birds is a book concerning them
RE heads a memo to mean 'concerning', straight out of the Latin
the flex running from a lamp to the wall

explanation.walkthrough: One word is asked for two answers, and the surface hides that by making 'repeatedly' sound like part of the noting rather than an instruction about the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something noted has been set down where it can be looked up again, which is what being on the record amounts to.

clue.text: Babbles, splatter splashing

indicators.note: Liquid that splashes lands in no pattern at all, so the letters it is thrown from land out of their order too.

parts.note: its eight letters, redistributed

explanation.walkthrough: The two long words sit together so naturally that the second reads as description rather than instruction, and the definition is left doing all its work in one word at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To prattle is to talk on and on about very little, which is what babbling is — chatter with the content taken out.

clue.text: Damaged sub with mortar: hear who's overseeing the boats?

indicators.note: Something damaged has been knocked out of shape, and letters knocked out of shape no longer sit where they were put.

parts.note: thirteen letters spread across those three words, rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hear' is the trap. Sitting after a colon it reads as an instruction to listen for a sound-alike, and it is raw material — four of the thirteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The official who runs a port — berths, moorings, the traffic in and out — has every boat in the place under their eye.

clue.text: Use your phone to find self-catering room with bill 50% reduced

parts.note: S/C is the abbreviation used in holiday listings for self-catering

indicators.note: 50% reduced means each word is cut to half its length, the end of room and the start of bill going

parts.note: the word room, losing half its letters
the word bill, losing half its letters

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker in a self-catering flat checks how much the half-price bill comes to on their phone.
explanation.walkthrough: Halving keeps RO from room and LL from bill.
explanation.definitionFit: To scroll is to move through the content on a phone screen with a finger, a common way of using one.

clue.text: Pop diva's entertaining, making a comeback, total cheese

indicators.note: To entertain guests is to have them in the house, so one piece is taken inside the other rather than laid beside it.

parts.note: the American singer of Believe, a one-name star since the sixties

indicators.note: A comeback is a return to where you started from, so the letters it governs are read back to front.

parts.note: to total a column of figures is to add them up, and it goes in backwards

explanation.walkthrough: 'Total cheese' is one insult on the surface — utter rubbish — and the setter has split it down the middle. Only the second word defines. The first is not telling you to do anything; it is a synonym standing in for letters, total in the sense a column of figures has.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the hard cow's-milk cheese named after a Somerset village, so it is one example of the class the definition names.

clue.text: Intelligence-gathering mission giving description of sunken ships, did you say?

indicators.note: The question asks about what was heard rather than what was written, so the letters follow the sound and not the spelling.

parts.note: sunken ships are wrecks, so a stretch of coast full of them is wrecky — and the W at the front of that word is silent

explanation.walkthrough: British forces shorten reconnaissance to five letters and say it 'recky', which is the whole clue: the wreck word loses nothing but its silent W on the way.
explanation.definitionFit: A recce is a reconnaissance — a quick look at the ground or the target before the real move — which is gathering intelligence in its plainest form.

clue.text: Kind of article mentioned

indicators.note: Here 'of' means part of: it points at letters lying inside the words that follow, rather than at a word that means the same as them.

parts.note: seven letters in a row, running across the join between the two words

explanation.walkthrough: Read straight, this is a sort of article that somebody brought up — and the only wordplay word in the whole clue is the tiny 'of'. 'Mentioned' is dressed as a homophone signal and is really just more of the hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: Clement weather is mild and a clement judge is merciful, so the word comes out as kind — gentle where it could be harsh.

clue.text: The Observer's heart?

definitions.meaning: a newspaper is the mouthpiece of a body or a cause, the word the trade uses for a house journal
the pump in your chest, one of the body's working parts

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are examples rather than synonyms, which is what the question mark is apologising for. A Sunday paper and a heart have nothing else whatever in common.
explanation.definitionFit: An organ is a publication speaking for a body — this paper is one — and also a working part of a body, which the heart is.

clue.text: Recreational vehicle inspired by piece of snooker equipment? That's unexpected

indicators.note: To inspire is to breathe in, so the thing named before it is drawn inside the thing named after it.

parts.note: the white one, the only ball a player is allowed to strike
RV is the American short form: the camper van you drive across a continent

explanation.walkthrough: Snooker is the wrong sport entirely — the answer comes off a baseball mound. The question mark is there because a table holds twenty-two balls and only one of them is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a pitch thrown to swerve away from where the batter expects it, so throwing somebody one means springing a surprise.

clue.text: Age of beermat regularly noted

indicators.note: Noting at regular intervals means writing down every second letter and letting the ones in between go past.

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth of its seven letters

explanation.walkthrough: A beermat is the cardboard coaster a pub glass stands on, and 'noted' slips by as part of that picture instead of the instruction it really is.
explanation.definitionFit: An era is a stretch of history with a character of its own — the Victorian one, the jet one — which is what calling something an age means.

clue.text: Behaved antisocially and gave birth

definitions.meaning: dropping rubbish in the street is the offence, and the verb for doing it comes straight off the noun
what a sow or a bitch does: the whole brood arrives together

explanation.surface: One person's bad week: they were antisocial, and then they gave birth.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are the same verb standing in two worlds — rubbish dropped on the pavement, and the moment a sow's whole brood arrives at once.
explanation.definitionFit: To litter is to strew rubbish about; an animal's litter is all the young born at one time, so bearing them is littering too.

clue.text: In Cuba and America, pretend to be one that can last a while without drink

definitions.text: one that can last a while without drink

indicators.note: in means the acting goes inside the letters for the two countries

parts.note: C is the international vehicle registration code for Cuba
US is short for the United States of America
to act is to pretend to be someone

explanation.surface: Someone playing a part in Cuba and the US manages without a drink for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drink' suggests a person on the wagon; the definition is a desert plant that stores water.
explanation.definitionFit: A cactus is a desert plant that stores water in its stems and survives long droughts.
